title: Stack applications: expression evaluation
lead: An Advanced section on evaluating expressions with stacks: reverse Polish notation with one stack, which is Essential, then ordinary infix expressions with two stacks, then unary and right-associative operators. Expressions are read character by character, and the only index is i, the position of the character the code is reading, counted from 0.
exercise_notes: The forth card is Exercism’s, with the 54 canonical cases the Exercism Python track runs as its tests and the track’s example as its Python reference; the JavaScript reference is written by the AI that built the section. The two Kattis cards keep their samples as source tests; their other tests and both references are written by the same AI. Kattis circuitmath has only its sample and is not built. TheAlgorithms’ postfix_evaluation, dijkstras_two_stack_algorithm and infix_to_postfix_conversion and tryalgo’s arithm_expr_eval carry tests but print no exercise statement, so they have no card. The Wikibooks reverse Polish traces and OpenDSA’s infix-to-postfix and postfix-evaluation exercises wait for an answer type that checks a sequence. Two pythonds self-checks are NC cards, kept in exercises-nc.json apart from the book’s CC BY-SA content; its third, postfix3, asks for a change to a function on a page this book only links, and its end-of-chapter exercises 2–5 and 10–13 print no answers, so they are left out. Kattis polish evaluates prefix expressions recursively and is held for chapter 4.

exercises.changes: The tests call evaluate with the list of input lines and expect the stack as a list, bottom first. As the Exercism Python track has it, a word with too few values on the stack raises StackUnderflowError, division by zero raises ZeroDivisionError, and an undefined word or the redefinition of a number raises ValueError.
exercises.prompt:
Implement an evaluator for a very simple subset of Forth. Forth is a stack-based programming language. Implement a very basic evaluator for a small subset of Forth. Your evaluator has to support the following words:
  • +, -, *, / (integer arithmetic)
  • DUP, DROP, SWAP, OVER (stack manipulation)
Your evaluator also has to support defining new words using the customary syntax: : word-name definition ;. To keep things simple the only data type you need to support is signed integers of at least 16 bits size. You should use the following rules for the syntax: a number is a sequence of one or more (ASCII) digits, a word is a sequence of one or more letters, digits, symbols or punctuation that is not a number. (Forth probably uses slightly different rules, but this is close enough.) Words are case-insensitive.

Input Input contains several test cases, one per line. Each test case consists of an expression to be evaluated, containing numbers, parentheses, and the operators $+,-,*,/$. Normal operator precedence applies, so multiplication and division bind harder than addition and subtraction. All operators evaluate left-to-right. Implicit multiplication is not possible, so $3(1+1)$ is not a valid input. There may be an arbitrary amount (including $0$) of spaces between tokens. Numbers are integers with absolute value at most $500$. Input is terminated by end of file. Output For each test case, output the value of the expression, with two digits of precision after the decimal point.

exercises.prompt: Two great friends, Eddie John and Kris Cross, are attending the Brackets Are Perfection Conference. They wholeheartedly agree with the main message of the conference and they are delighted with all the new things they learn about brackets. One of these things is a bracket sequence. If you want to do a computation with $+$ and $\times $, you usually write it like so: $$ (2 \times (2 + 1 + 0 + 1) \times 1) + 3 + 2. $$ The brackets are only used to group multiplications and additions together. This means that you can remove all the operators, as long as you remember that addition is used for numbers outside any parentheses! A bracket sequence can then be shortened to $$ (\; 2 \; ( \; 2 \; 1 \; 0 \; 1 \; ) \; 1 \; ) \; 3 \; 2. $$ That is much better, because it saves on writing all those operators. Reading bracket sequences is easy, too. Suppose you have the following bracket sequence You start with addition, so this is the same as the following: $$ 5 + 2 + (\; 3 \; 1 \; (\; 2 \; 2 \; ) \; ( \; 3 \; 3 \; ) \; 1 \; ). $$ You know the parentheses group a multiplication, so this is equal to $$ 5 + 2 + (3 \times 1 \times (\; 2 \; 2 \; ) \times ( \; 3 \; 3 \; ) \times 1). $$ Then there is another level of parentheses: that groups an operation within a multiplication, so the operation must be addition. $$ 5 + 2 + (3 \times 1 \times (2 + 2 ) \times (3 + 3) \times 1 ) = 5 + 2 + (3 \times 1 \times 4 \times 6 \times 1) = 5+2 + 72 = 79. $$ Since bracket sequences are so much easier than normal expressions with operators, it should be easy to evaluate some big ones. We will even allow you to write a program to do it for you. Note that $(\; )$ is not a valid bracket sequence, nor a subsequence of any valid bracket sequence. Input One line containing a single integer $1\leq n\leq 3\cdot 10^5$. One line consisting of $n$ tokens, each being either (, ), or an integer $0\leq x \lt 10^9+7$. It is guaranteed that the tokens form a bracket sequence. Output Output the value of the given bracket sequence. Since this may be very large, you should print it modulo $10^9+7$.

answer.grow: (n, rand) => { const t = []; let d = 0; for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) { const r = rand(); if (r < 0.3) { t.push('('); d++; t.push(String(rand.int(0, 9))); } else if (r < 0.5 && d > 0) { t.push(')'); d--; } else t.push(String(rand.int(0, 9))); } while (d-- > 0) t.push(')'); return t.length + '\n' + t.join(' ') + '\n'; }
